metadata.title: Sri Lankan Tea Knowledge Corpus
metadata.description: Comprehensive dataset for RAG-based tea information retrieval
metadata.source: Tea Research Institute of Sri Lanka (TRI), Ceylon Tea Board, Academic Literature, Ceylon Tea Board Official Publications, TRI Circulars, Wikipedia API (Auto-Scraped)

documents.title: TRI 2025 - Most Popular Sri Lankan Tea Cultivar
documents.content: TRI 2025 is the most widely cultivated tea variety in Sri Lanka, developed by the Tea Research Institute. This Cambod-type cultivar originated from the ASM 4/10 clone and was released for commercial planting due to its exceptional adaptability. TRI 2025 demonstrates remarkable versatility, thriving in low country, mid country, and up country elevations. The cultivar exhibits strong resistance to blister blight disease caused by Exobasidium vexans and shows tolerance to root-lesion nematode (Pratylenchus loosi). Additionally, TRI 2025 possesses drought tolerance, making it suitable for regions with irregular rainfall patterns. The tea produced from this cultivar has a well-balanced flavor profile suitable for both orthodox and CTC processing methods.

documents.title: TRI 2043 - Purple Tea Cultivar
documents.content: TRI 2043 is a unique cultivar known for its distinctive purple-pigmented leaves due to high anthocyanin content. This special characteristic makes it valuable for producing specialty teas including Golden Tips and Purple Tea. The anthocyanins provide additional antioxidant properties beyond regular green tea catechins. TRI 2043 is particularly suited for mid country and up country cultivation, especially in the Uva region where the unique climatic conditions enhance its special characteristics. The cultivar shows good resistance to blister blight and produces teas with exceptional aroma and flavor complexity. Purple tea from TRI 2043 commands premium prices in international markets due to its rarity and health benefits.

documents.title: TRI 2026 - High Yield Cultivar
documents.content: TRI 2026 is recognized for its high yield potential and good quality black tea production. This cultivar performs exceptionally well in low country and mid country regions of Sri Lanka. It produces leaves with good fermentation characteristics, resulting in teas with bright liquor and pleasant aroma. TRI 2026 has moderate resistance to blister blight and nematode attacks. The cultivar's vigorous growth habit and good recovery after pruning make it economically attractive for commercial plantations. It is particularly popular among smallholders due to its consistent yield performance.

documents.title: TRI 2023 - Quality Black Tea Producer
documents.content: TRI 2023 is valued for producing high-quality black tea with excellent cup characteristics. This cultivar is best suited for mid country and up country cultivation where cooler temperatures enhance tea quality. TRI 2023 produces medium yields but compensates with superior made tea quality. The cultivar has moderate resistance to blister blight but is susceptible to nematode damage in heavily infested soils. Teas from TRI 2023 are known for their bright infusion, good strength, and pleasant flavor, making them popular for single-origin premium teas.

documents.title: TRI 3013 - Aromatic Up Country Cultivar
documents.content: TRI 3013 belongs to the TRI 3000 series and is specifically developed for up country conditions. This cultivar is celebrated for producing teas with exceptional aroma and delicate flavor characteristics. TRI 3013 shows strong resistance to blister blight, which is particularly important in the misty, humid conditions of high elevations where this disease thrives. The cultivar produces smaller, finer leaves that are ideal for premium grade production. Teas from TRI 3013 are often used in specialty blends and single-estate offerings due to their distinctive aromatic qualities.

documents.title: TRI 3019 - Highly Disease Resistant Cultivar
documents.content: TRI 3019 stands out for its exceptional resistance to blister blight, rated as highly resistant compared to other cultivars. This makes it invaluable for cultivation in high-elevation areas where blister blight pressure is intense. The cultivar also demonstrates good yield potential and produces quality black tea. TRI 3019 is suitable for both up country and mid country regions and has become increasingly popular as plantations seek to reduce fungicide applications. The tea quality is characterized by good brightness and moderate strength.

documents.title: TRI 4006 - Premium Up Country Cultivar
documents.content: TRI 4006 represents the advanced TRI 4000 series and is known for excellent quality combined with high yield potential. This cultivar is highly resistant to both blister blight and nematode attacks, providing dual protection against major tea pests in Sri Lanka. TRI 4006 is recommended specifically for up country cultivation where it produces teas with superior cup quality. The leaves have good processing characteristics for orthodox manufacture. Estates using TRI 4006 report consistent quality and reduced crop protection costs.

documents.title: TRI 4052 - Nematode Tolerant Cultivar
documents.content: TRI 4052 was specifically developed to address the significant nematode problem in Sri Lankan tea lands. The cultivar shows high tolerance to root-lesion nematode (Pratylenchus loosi), which causes substantial yield losses in susceptible varieties. TRI 4052 is recommended for low country and mid country regions where nematode populations tend to be high. The cultivar produces good yields and acceptable tea quality, making it a practical choice for replanting nematode-infested fields without requiring expensive soil treatment.

documents.title: TRI 4053 - Multiple Pest Resistant Cultivar
documents.content: TRI 4053 offers multiple pest resistance characteristics, showing both blister blight resistance and high nematode tolerance. This combination makes it particularly valuable for integrated pest management approaches in tea cultivation. The cultivar is suited for low country and mid country regions and produces good quality tea with satisfactory yields. TRI 4053 is increasingly recommended for new plantings and replanting programs where reducing chemical inputs is a priority. The cultivar's broad resistance spectrum provides economic benefits through reduced crop protection costs.

documents.title: TRI 5001 - Latest Generation High Yielder
documents.content: TRI 5001 is part of the newest TRI 5000 series released in 2019, representing the latest advances in tea breeding. This cultivar offers 10-15% yield improvement over previous generations while maintaining high tea quality. TRI 5001 shows resistance to blister blight and notably to shot hole borer (Euwallacea fornicatus), a significant pest. The cultivar is recommended for up country regions and produces tea with bright liquor and good flavor. Early adopters report excellent field performance and quality premiums at auction.

documents.title: TRI 5002 - Excellent Quality New Release
documents.content: TRI 5002, released alongside TRI 5001 in 2019, is noted for producing tea of excellent quality. The cultivar shows highly resistant characteristics against blister blight but has some susceptibility to shot hole borer. TRI 5002 is specifically recommended for up country cultivation where its quality potential can be fully realized. The tea produced has exceptional brightness, aroma, and flavor complexity that commands premium prices. This cultivar is ideal for estates focusing on specialty and single-origin market segments.

documents.title: TRI 5003 - Nematode Tolerant New Generation
documents.content: TRI 5003 combines the yield advantages of the TRI 5000 series with high nematode tolerance inherited from earlier breeding lines. This cultivar addresses the continuing need for nematode-resistant varieties in Sri Lankan tea lands. TRI 5003 is suitable for both up country and mid country regions and also shows good blister blight resistance. The dual resistance characteristics make it valuable for areas where both pests are present. Tea quality is good, and yields meet the enhanced expectations of the 5000 series.

documents.title: TRI 5004 - Balanced Performance Cultivar
documents.content: TRI 5004 completes the initial TRI 5000 series release, offering balanced performance across yield, quality, and disease resistance parameters. The cultivar shows good blister blight resistance and moderate nematode tolerance. TRI 5004 is recommended for up country cultivation and produces tea with consistent quality characteristics. This cultivar is suitable for estates seeking reliable performance without extreme specialization in any single trait. It represents a safe choice for diversified planting programs.

documents.title: Estate Selections - DN, DG7, DT1, DUN7
documents.content: Beyond TRI cultivars, several estate selections have proven commercially valuable in Sri Lanka. DN (Deniyaya Selection) originated from the Deniyaya region and shows local adaptation. DG7 is well-suited for low country conditions with good yield potential. DT1 stands out for its drought tolerance, making it valuable for areas with unreliable rainfall. DUN7 (Dun 7 Selection) is an established estate selection with proven performance. These selections complement TRI varieties and provide genetic diversity in commercial plantings.

documents.title: Nuwara Eliya - The Champagne of Ceylon Tea
documents.content: Nuwara Eliya, often called 'Little England', produces the most delicate and prized Ceylon teas. Located at an average elevation of 1,868 meters (6,128 feet), it represents the highest tea-growing region in Sri Lanka. The cool climate, with temperatures rarely exceeding 20°C, results in slow leaf growth that concentrates flavor compounds. Nuwara Eliya teas are characterized by their exceptionally light, golden liquor with greenish-yellow tones - the lightest of all Ceylon teas. The flavor profile features exquisite bouquet with delicate fragrance, brightness, and briskness. Distinctive notes of cypress, wild mint, and eucalyptus distinguish these teas. The Western Quality Season from January to March and Eastern Quality Season in August-September produce the finest teas when cool, dry winds enhance quality. Nuwara Eliya tea is often compared to Champagne in the wine world - representing the pinnacle of Ceylon tea excellence.

documents.title: Dimbula - Classic High Grown Character
documents.content: Dimbula is one of the most celebrated high-grown tea districts in Sri Lanka, with elevations ranging from 1,100 to 1,700 meters (3,500-5,500 feet). The region was among the earliest districts planted with tea after the coffee blight devastated plantations in the 1870s. Dimbula teas are renowned for their fine golden-orange hue, brightness, and refreshingly mellow character with hints of jasmine and cypress. The body ranges from medium to full, making these teas versatile for various brewing preferences. The Quality Season from January to April, during the dry period influenced by the southwest monsoon, produces the most sought-after Dimbula teas. The region's combination of altitude, rainfall pattern, and soil creates ideal conditions for producing teas with excellent keeping qualities and consistent character that has made Dimbula a benchmark for Ceylon high-grown teas.

documents.title: Uva - Unique Monsoon-Influenced Teas
documents.content: Uva is a distinctive tea region producing some of the most exotic Ceylon teas due to its unique exposure to both the northeast and southwest monsoons. Located on the eastern slopes of the central highlands at 1,000-1,600 meters (3,000-5,000 feet), Uva experiences weather patterns unlike any other tea region. The famous Uva Season from July to September occurs when the Cachan wind - a dry wind from the northeast monsoon - sweeps across the region, causing leaves to dehydrate slightly on the bush. This natural withering concentrates flavor compounds, producing teas with distinctive mellow, smooth, and exotic aromatic character. The bright, coppery liquor and unique flavor profile have made Uva teas highly prized. Thomas Lipton famously introduced Americans to tea using Uva teas, establishing the region's international reputation. Uva teas are particularly valued in Middle Eastern and European markets.

documents.title: Uda Pussellawa - Distinctive Eastern Highland Teas
documents.content: Uda Pussellawa lies adjacent to Nuwara Eliya on the eastern slopes of Sri Lanka's central highlands. The region produces teas that share some characteristics with Nuwara Eliya but with their own distinctive character. The eastern exposure means Uda Pussellawa experiences different weather patterns, particularly during the monsoon transitions. Teas from this region have medium body with rose-like notes and a delicate astringency. The quality season aligns with the dry period when southeast winds prevail. Uda Pussellawa teas are known for their pinkish hue when brewed and subtle complexity. While less well-known internationally than Nuwara Eliya or Uva, Uda Pussellawa produces excellent teas that are gaining recognition among connoisseurs seeking distinctive Ceylon origins.

documents.title: Kandy - The Original Ceylon Tea District
documents.content: Kandy, the ancient royal capital of Sri Lanka, holds special significance in tea history as the region where commercial tea cultivation began. Situated at 600-1,200 meters (2,000-4,000 feet) in the mid country zone, Kandy produces medium-grown teas with distinctive character. The relatively lower elevation compared to high-grown regions results in faster leaf growth and more robust teas. Kandy teas are characterized by bright infusion with coppery tones, strong and malty flavor, and full body. These teas are particularly popular for morning drinking and pair well with milk. The region's rich biodiversity and traditional plucking methods contribute to consistent quality. Kandy teas represent excellent value, offering good strength and flavor without the premium prices of high-grown teas.

documents.title: Ruhuna - Bold Low Country Character
documents.content: Ruhuna encompasses the southern low country tea districts including Galle and Matara, producing distinctively bold teas at elevations from sea level to 600 meters (2,000 feet). The warmer climate accelerates leaf growth, resulting in larger leaves with different chemical composition than highland teas. Ruhuna teas are characterized by dark, strong liquor and bold, robust flavor - quite different from the delicacy of high-grown teas. These characteristics make Ruhuna teas ideal for blending, where they provide body, strength, and color to create balanced commercial blends. The teas also perform well with milk and sugar, popular in traditional tea preparations. Low country production represents a significant portion of Sri Lanka's total tea output and supports many smallholder farmers in the southern regions.

documents.title: Sabaragamuwa - Emerging Low Country Quality
documents.content: Sabaragamuwa is a low country tea region that has gained recognition for producing quality teas despite its lower elevation. Located in the wet zone of southwestern Sri Lanka, the region benefits from abundant rainfall and rich soils. Sabaragamuwa teas typically have medium to full body with hints of caramel and spice. The region is known for both orthodox and CTC production, with many smallholders contributing to overall output. Modern processing techniques and improved cultivars have enhanced the quality reputation of Sabaragamuwa teas. The region represents good value for everyday drinking teas while some estates produce premium grades that rival mid country teas in quality.

documents.title: Elevation Categories and Tea Quality
documents.content: Sri Lankan tea is classified into three elevation categories that fundamentally influence tea character. High Grown (Up Country) teas from above 1,200 meters produce the most delicate, complex, and prized teas with light liquor and subtle flavors. Medium Grown (Mid Country) teas from 600-1,200 meters balance body and flavor, producing versatile teas with good strength and character. Low Grown (Low Country) teas from below 600 meters produce bold, strong teas ideal for blending and traditional preparations. The elevation effect relates to temperature - cooler temperatures slow leaf growth, allowing accumulation of flavor compounds, amino acids, and aromatic substances. Higher elevation teas command premium prices, while low elevation teas provide volume and strength for commercial blends. The Lion Logo certification on Ceylon tea guarantees origin and quality standards regardless of elevation category.

documents.title: Orange Pekoe (OP) - Premier Whole Leaf Grade
documents.content: Orange Pekoe (OP) is the highest main grade of whole leaf Ceylon tea, representing the standard for quality leaf tea production. Despite its name, Orange Pekoe contains no orange flavoring - the term likely derives from the Dutch House of Orange or the copper color of oxidized leaf. OP consists of long, wiry, thin leaves that are carefully rolled to preserve their integrity. The leaves unfurl beautifully when brewed, releasing delicate fragrance and producing a light to medium bodied infusion. OP teas are prized for their smooth character without bitterness when properly brewed. This grade is typically produced from the youngest leaves and represents careful plucking and processing standards. OP is the benchmark grade against which other whole leaf grades are compared.

documents.title: Orange Pekoe 1 (OP1) - Superior Whole Leaf
documents.content: Orange Pekoe 1 (OP1) represents a higher quality tier within the Orange Pekoe classification, distinguished by greater tip content and more careful leaf selection. The '1' designation indicates superior sorting and quality control during processing. OP1 leaves tend to be more uniform in size and appearance with visible golden or silver tips indicating young leaf shoots. When brewed, OP1 produces a more refined infusion than standard OP with enhanced aroma and brightness. This grade commands premium prices at auction and is sought after for single-origin presentations where leaf appearance and cup quality both matter. OP1 is particularly associated with high-grown regions where growing conditions favor tip development.

documents.title: Flowery Orange Pekoe (FOP) - Tippy Whole Leaf
documents.content: Flowery Orange Pekoe (FOP) is a whole leaf grade characterized by the presence of tips or buds mixed with the leaves. The term 'flowery' refers to the tips, which were historically called 'flowers' in tea terminology. Tips are the unopened leaf buds that contain high concentrations of flavor compounds and appear as golden or silvery strands among the darker leaves. FOP indicates careful plucking of young shoots and gentle processing to preserve the delicate tips. The presence of tips enhances both visual appeal and cup quality, contributing aromatic complexity and sweetness. FOP grades are premium offerings that showcase the finest plucking standards of an estate.

documents.title: Tippy Golden Flowery Orange Pekoe (TGFOP)
documents.content: Tippy Golden Flowery Orange Pekoe (TGFOP) represents an elite grade with exceptional tip content. The 'Tippy' designation indicates an abundance of golden tips throughout the leaf, while 'Golden' describes the color of these tips from young leaf buds. TGFOP is among the highest grades of whole leaf tea and commands significant premiums. The high tip content results from selective plucking of only the finest shoots and careful processing to preserve tip integrity. When brewed, TGFOP produces complex, aromatic infusions with natural sweetness and refined character. This grade is typically reserved for special productions and limited releases from premium estates.

documents.title: Broken Orange Pekoe (BOP) - Main Broken Grade
documents.content: Broken Orange Pekoe (BOP) is the principal broken leaf grade and represents the largest category of Ceylon tea production by volume. During orthodox processing, leaves are broken to create smaller particles that brew more quickly and produce stronger infusions than whole leaf grades. BOP consists of well-made broken leaves without excessive dust or fiber. The grade produces a brisk, bright infusion with good strength and color - characteristics valued in everyday drinking teas. BOP is popular for commercial tea bags and loose tea blends. The breaking process actually releases more flavor compounds quickly, making BOP efficient for producing satisfying cups in standard brewing times.

documents.title: Broken Orange Pekoe 1 (BOP1) - Premium Broken
documents.content: Broken Orange Pekoe 1 (BOP1) is a superior broken leaf grade with wiry, medium-length particles. The '1' designation indicates higher quality standards in selection and processing. BOP1 is characterized by malty flavor notes and golden infusion color when brewed. This grade often comes from high-grown regions where smaller leaves produce more concentrated flavor when broken. BOP1 represents excellent value, offering much of the quality character of whole leaf teas with the convenience and strength of broken grades. It is popular for premium tea bag production and quality loose tea offerings.

documents.title: Flowery Broken Orange Pekoe (FBOP)
documents.content: Flowery Broken Orange Pekoe (FBOP) combines the strength of broken leaf tea with the quality enhancement of tip content. This grade contains visible tips mixed with well-made broken leaves, indicating fine plucking standards despite the broken format. FBOP produces strong, bright infusions with added complexity from the tips. The coarser leaf structure compared to fannings allows controlled brewing without excessive bitterness. FBOP is valued for quality blends and premium tea bag production where both strength and character are important. High-grown FBOP commands premium prices at auction.

documents.title: Broken Orange Pekoe Fannings (BOPF) - Main Sri Lankan Grade
documents.content: Broken Orange Pekoe Fannings (BOPF) is the most important commercial grade in Sri Lankan tea production, accounting for the largest share of exports. Fannings are smaller particles than broken grades, created during the sorting process. Despite their small size, quality BOPF produces rich, bright liquor with good color and satisfying strength. The small particle size allows quick brewing, making BOPF ideal for tea bags where consumers expect rapid flavor extraction. Sri Lankan BOPF is renowned internationally for its quality, representing excellent value for everyday tea drinking. The grade performs well with milk and sugar in traditional tea preparations.

documents.title: Flowery Broken Orange Pekoe Fannings (FBOPF)
documents.content: Flowery Broken Orange Pekoe Fannings (FBOPF) is considered one of the best fannings grades available, combining small particle convenience with tip content for enhanced quality. The presence of tips in a fannings grade is notable and indicates high-quality source leaf and careful processing. FBOPF produces bright, flavorful infusions quickly while offering more complexity than standard fannings. This grade is popular for premium tea bag production where manufacturers want to offer superior cup quality in a convenient format. FBOPF from high-grown regions is particularly prized.

documents.title: Silver Tips - The Pinnacle of Ceylon Tea
documents.content: Silver Tips represents the absolute pinnacle of Ceylon tea production, consisting entirely of unopened leaf buds hand-plucked before sunrise. The silvery-white appearance comes from fine downy hairs covering the young buds, which measure at least 2.5 centimeters in length. Production requires extraordinary labor - approximately 5 kilograms of fresh buds yield just 1 kilogram of finished Silver Tips. The buds are minimally processed to preserve their delicate character, resulting in tea that produces an almost colorless to very pale gold infusion. The flavor profile is remarkably subtle with hints of pine, honey, and delicate floral notes. Silver Tips commands the highest prices of any Ceylon tea and is produced in very limited quantities. It is traditionally enjoyed without milk to appreciate its delicate nuances.

documents.title: Golden Tips - Amber Excellence
documents.content: Golden Tips is a premium grade similar to Silver Tips but with distinctive golden coloration of the buds. This color typically develops from specific cultivars, particularly TRI 2043, or from slight withering that allows oxidation to begin. Golden Tips produces a pale amber to golden infusion with more pronounced flavor than Silver Tips while retaining exceptional delicacy. The flavor profile often includes notes of rose, peach, citrus, and honey. Like Silver Tips, Golden Tips requires meticulous hand-plucking and minimal processing. Production is limited and commands premium prices second only to Silver Tips. Golden Tips is particularly associated with estates in the Nuwara Eliya and Uva regions.

documents.title: Pekoe (P) - Traditional Whole Leaf
documents.content: Pekoe (P) is a whole leaf grade consisting of shorter, more tightly rolled leaves than Orange Pekoe. The term 'pekoe' derives from Chinese 'pak-ho' meaning white down, referring to the fine hairs on young tea leaves. In grading, Pekoe represents good quality whole leaf without the length and wiriness of OP. The shorter leaves produce a slightly stronger infusion with a hint of pleasant bitterness that some tea drinkers prefer. Pekoe is less common than it once was as production has shifted toward other grades, but it remains an important traditional classification in tea grading systems.

documents.title: Dust Grades - Fine Particle Teas
documents.content: Dust grades represent the finest particles in tea grading, smaller even than fannings. Despite their unglamorous name, quality dust can produce excellent cup results. The main dust grades include D (Dust), D1 (Dust 1), and PD (Pekoe Dust). These grades brew almost instantly and produce very strong, deeply colored infusions. Dust is extensively used in tea bags, particularly for economy products where quick brewing and strength are priorities. While dust lacks the subtlety of larger grades, it efficiently delivers the stimulating and flavorful aspects of tea. Sri Lankan dust grades are considered among the best in the world for their clean taste without excessive bitterness.

documents.title: Orthodox Tea Manufacturing Process
documents.content: Orthodox processing is the traditional method of tea manufacture that Sri Lanka has made its specialty, accounting for 95% of the country's production. The process begins with plucking, ideally two leaves and a bud. Withering follows, lasting 12-20 hours to reduce moisture content by approximately 50%, making leaves pliable for rolling. Rolling is a critical step lasting 30-60 minutes that breaks cell walls, releases enzymes, and creates the characteristic twisted leaf shape. During oxidation (often incorrectly called fermentation), enzymes convert catechins to theaflavins and thearubigins over 2-4 hours under controlled temperature and humidity. Finally, drying halts oxidation and reduces moisture to approximately 3% for shelf stability. Orthodox processing produces complex, layered flavors with distinct regional character that distinguishes Ceylon tea in world markets.

documents.title: CTC Tea Manufacturing Process
documents.content: CTC (Crush, Tear, Curl) is a mechanized processing method invented by Sir William McKercher in 1931. Unlike orthodox processing which preserves leaf integrity, CTC uses serrated rollers to cut leaves into small, uniform particles. The process is much faster than orthodox, taking only 2-3 hours from fresh leaf to finished tea. CTC produces small, hard pellets that brew quickly with bold, strong flavor. This processing method dominates global tea production, accounting for approximately 95% of world output, though Sri Lanka maintains its focus on orthodox. CTC tea is ideal for tea bags, iced tea, and masala chai where quick brewing and strength are valued over subtle complexity. Some Sri Lankan estates produce CTC for specific market demands.

documents.title: Withering - The First Critical Step
documents.content: Withering is the first processing step after plucking and fundamentally influences final tea quality. Fresh tea leaves contain approximately 75-80% moisture, which must be reduced to around 50-55% for proper rolling. Physical withering makes leaves soft and pliable, preventing breakage during rolling. Chemical withering initiates important biochemical changes including caffeine redistribution and aroma compound development. Withering typically takes 12-20 hours in Sri Lankan factories, though this varies with weather conditions and desired tea character. Under-withered leaf produces greenish, harsh tea, while over-withered leaf yields flat, lifeless character. Modern factories use withering troughs with controlled airflow to achieve consistent results.

documents.title: Rolling and Oxidation Explained
documents.content: Rolling serves multiple purposes in orthodox tea manufacture. The mechanical action breaks cell walls, releasing enzymes and substrates that will interact during oxidation. Rolling also shapes the leaves into their characteristic twisted appearance and releases leaf juices onto the surface where oxidation occurs. The rolling process typically involves 30-60 minutes in specialized rolling machines. Oxidation follows rolling, during which polyphenol oxidase enzymes convert catechins to theaflavins (bright, brisk character) and thearubigins (color, body). Oxidation occurs at 20-30°C with 95-98% humidity over 2-4 hours, carefully monitored to achieve desired character. The factory manager determines the optimal oxidation point based on color change and aroma development.

documents.title: Tea Drying and Sorting
documents.content: Drying halts oxidation at the precise point determined by the factory manager, fixing the chemical composition that determines tea character. Hot air dryers reduce moisture content from approximately 50% to just 3%, ensuring shelf stability. The drying temperature must be carefully controlled - too hot and the tea develops harsh, burnt notes; too cool and enzymatic activity continues, altering character. After drying, tea undergoes sorting through a series of sieves that separate different particle sizes into grades. Electrostatic sorters remove fiber and stalk. Color sorting may remove off-colored particles. The sorting process determines the final grade designations and ensures uniformity within each grade. Proper sorting is essential for consistent brew quality.

documents.title: Tea Types by Oxidation Level
documents.content: Tea types are fundamentally distinguished by oxidation level during processing. White tea undergoes minimal oxidation (0-5%), with leaves simply withered and dried, preserving the highest antioxidant levels. Green tea is not oxidized (0%); leaves are quickly heated by pan-firing or steaming to deactivate enzymes, preserving green color and high EGCG content. Oolong tea is partially oxidized (15-85%), creating complex flavor profiles between green and black tea. Black tea is fully oxidized (100%), producing characteristic dark color and bold flavor from theaflavins and thearubigins. Sri Lanka produces primarily black tea through the orthodox method, though small quantities of green, white, and oolong are also manufactured for niche markets.

documents.title: EGCG - The Master Antioxidant in Tea
documents.content: Epigallocatechin-3-gallate (EGCG) is the most abundant and potent catechin in tea, representing approximately 59% of total catechins. A typical 240ml cup of green tea contains approximately 187mg of EGCG. Research has established EGCG as a more powerful antioxidant than vitamins C and E, capable of neutralizing harmful free radicals that damage cells. The compound demonstrates anti-inflammatory properties and has been studied extensively for potential health benefits including cardiovascular protection, neuroprotection, and metabolic enhancement. EGCG's antioxidant capacity is measured at approximately 25-100 times more potent than vitamins C and E in some assays. Processing affects EGCG content - green tea retains the most, while black tea converts some EGCG to theaflavins during oxidation, which have their own beneficial properties.

documents.title: Catechins - Tea's Polyphenol Family
documents.content: Catechins are a family of polyphenolic compounds that comprise 18-36% of tea's dry weight and are responsible for many health benefits. The four major catechins are EGCG (epigallocatechin gallate), ECG (epicatechin gallate), EGC (epigallocatechin), and EC (epicatechin). Their antioxidant potency ranks approximately EGCG ≈ ECG > EGC > EC. Catechins contribute to tea's characteristic astringency and are more abundant in young leaves - another reason why fine plucking produces healthier tea. During black tea production, catechins partially convert to theaflavins and thearubigins through oxidation. Green tea retains more original catechins, while black tea offers different but still beneficial polyphenol profiles. Regular tea consumption providing 200-300mg of catechins daily is associated with positive health outcomes.

documents.title: L-Theanine - Tea's Calming Amino Acid
documents.content: L-theanine is a unique amino acid found almost exclusively in the tea plant (Camellia sinensis). This compound produces calming effects without drowsiness by promoting alpha brain wave activity associated with relaxed alertness. L-theanine works synergistically with tea's caffeine - the theanine smooths caffeine's stimulating effects, providing alert focus without the jitters associated with coffee. Research indicates L-theanine may improve cognitive function, reduce stress and anxiety, and enhance sleep quality. Shade-grown teas like Japanese gyokuro have higher L-theanine content as shade increases amino acid accumulation. A typical cup of tea contains 25-60mg of L-theanine. The combination of L-theanine and caffeine in tea creates a unique mental state prized by meditators and scholars throughout history.

documents.title: Cardiovascular Benefits of Tea Consumption
documents.content: Regular tea consumption has been consistently associated with improved cardiovascular health in epidemiological studies. Tea polyphenols help reduce LDL cholesterol oxidation, a key step in atherosclerotic plaque formation. Studies show tea consumption improves endothelial function, helping blood vessels dilate properly. Meta-analyses indicate that drinking 3 or more cups of tea daily is associated with reduced risk of heart attack and stroke. The mechanisms include antioxidant protection of blood vessel walls, mild blood pressure reduction, improved lipid profiles, and anti-inflammatory effects. Both green and black tea show cardiovascular benefits, though the specific compounds differ. The evidence is strong enough that some health authorities recognize tea as part of a heart-healthy diet.

documents.title: Tea and Cognitive Function
documents.content: Tea consumption has been linked to improved cognitive function and reduced risk of cognitive decline. A Singapore longitudinal study found regular tea drinkers had 64% lower risk of cognitive impairment compared to non-tea drinkers. The combination of caffeine and L-theanine provides sustained attention and improved performance on cognitive tasks. Long-term benefits may include neuroprotection from tea polyphenols that cross the blood-brain barrier. EGCG has shown potential in laboratory studies to protect neurons from damage associated with Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases. The ritual of tea preparation and consumption may also provide cognitive benefits through mindfulness. Regular moderate tea consumption appears to support brain health throughout the lifespan.

documents.title: Tea Polyphenols and Metabolic Health
documents.content: Research indicates tea polyphenols may support metabolic health through multiple mechanisms. EGCG has been shown to enhance fat oxidation during exercise and at rest. Some studies suggest green tea consumption modestly increases metabolic rate. Tea polyphenols may improve insulin sensitivity and help regulate blood glucose levels. Anti-inflammatory effects of tea compounds reduce chronic low-grade inflammation associated with metabolic syndrome. Clinical trials have shown modest weight management benefits from tea consumption, particularly green tea. The effects are most pronounced when combined with healthy diet and exercise. While not a magic solution for weight loss, regular tea consumption appears to support overall metabolic function.

documents.title: Safe Tea Consumption Guidelines
documents.content: Health authorities generally consider 3-5 cups of tea daily safe and potentially beneficial for most adults. This consumption level provides meaningful polyphenol intake without excessive caffeine. A typical cup of black tea contains 40-70mg caffeine, compared to 95-200mg in coffee. Individual caffeine sensitivity varies, and some people may need to limit consumption, especially later in the day to avoid sleep disruption. Pregnant women are advised to limit caffeine intake to 200mg daily. Very high tea consumption (10+ cups daily) may interfere with iron absorption, particularly if consumed with meals. Tea is best enjoyed between meals rather than with iron-rich foods. Quality tea from reputable sources minimizes risk of contaminants.

documents.title: Theaflavins and Thearubigins in Black Tea
documents.content: Theaflavins and thearubigins are polyphenolic compounds unique to oxidized teas like black tea. They form when catechins undergo enzymatic oxidation during processing. Theaflavins contribute bright, brisk characteristics and orange-red color to black tea liquor. Thearubigins provide the deep reddish-brown color and body. While these compounds have less direct antioxidant activity than catechins, research shows they provide their own health benefits including cholesterol management and antiviral properties. Black tea consumption has been associated with cardiovascular benefits in large population studies, indicating theaflavins and thearubigins contribute meaningfully to tea's health profile. Black tea remains a significant source of beneficial polyphenols despite oxidation changing the catechin profile.

documents.title: Fine Plucking - Two Leaves and a Bud Standard
documents.content: Fine plucking of two leaves and a bud represents the gold standard for quality tea production in Sri Lanka. This plucking standard, known locally as 'two and a bud', ensures optimal balance between quality and yield. The bud contains the highest concentration of flavor compounds, amino acids, and polyphenols. The two young leaves adjacent to the bud are tender with good chemical composition. This combination produces tea with brightness, complexity, and strength. Fine plucking requires skilled labor - pluckers must select only shoots at the right stage while leaving others to develop. Tea Research Institute guidelines recommend maintaining 75% fine leaf composition by weight in harvested material. Estates focusing on premium production enforce strict plucking standards.

documents.title: Imperial Plucking for Silver Tips
documents.content: Imperial plucking refers to harvesting only the unopened bud without any leaves - the most selective plucking standard. This practice is reserved exclusively for producing Silver Tips and the finest white teas. Imperial plucking must occur in early morning before buds open, typically before sunrise when dew still covers the plants. The technique requires extraordinary skill to remove only the bud without damaging the plant. Yield is extremely low - approximately 5 kilograms of fresh buds produce just 1 kilogram of finished Silver Tips. Only certain cultivars produce suitable buds, and weather conditions must be ideal. The resulting tea commands the highest prices in the world, making imperial plucking economically viable despite its labor intensity.

documents.title: Coarse Plucking and Quality Impact
documents.content: Coarse plucking refers to harvesting shoots with more than three leaves, often including mature leaves and woody stems. This practice severely compromises tea quality and is considered a reject category in premium production. Mature leaves have high fiber content and low concentrations of desirable compounds like catechins and amino acids. Woody stems add harshness and astringency without flavor contribution. Coarse plucked material produces tea with poor brightness, harsh character, and weak aroma. In quality assessment, coarse plucking is penalized heavily - the AI grading system assigns 0 points (reject) to coarse plucked material. Factors leading to coarse plucking include labor shortages, payment systems based on weight alone, and poor supervision. Quality-focused estates implement strict monitoring to minimize coarse plucking.

documents.title: Plucking Round and Bush Recovery
documents.content: Plucking round refers to the interval between successive harvests from the same area. In Sri Lanka, plucking rounds typically range from 7-10 days depending on season and elevation. Shorter rounds during flush periods ensure tender shoots are harvested at optimal development. Longer rounds allow adequate recovery and new growth. The plucking table - the maintained surface of the tea bush from which shoots emerge - must be kept clean and level for uniform shoot development. Proper plucking technique removes shoots cleanly without damaging dormant buds that will produce the next flush. Over-plucking or plucking too close damages the plant. Under-plucking leaves shoots to become coarse. Skilled pluckers balance harvest intensity with plant health for sustained productivity.

documents.title: Machine vs Hand Plucking
documents.content: The debate between machine and hand plucking involves trade-offs between cost efficiency and quality. Hand plucking allows selective harvest of shoots at optimal development, maintaining fine plucking standards. Skilled pluckers can achieve high fine leaf percentages impossible with machines. However, labor costs make hand plucking increasingly expensive. Mechanical harvesters cut all shoots above a certain height regardless of development stage. This produces mixed quality harvest including both fine and coarse material. Machine plucking is more common in low-elevation, high-yield situations where volume matters more than premium quality. In Sri Lanka, hand plucking predominates for quality production, particularly in high-grown regions. Some estates use selective mechanization for maintenance rounds while hand-plucking during quality seasons.

documents.title: Blister Blight - Most Severe Leaf Disease
documents.content: Blister blight caused by Exobasidium vexans is the most economically important leaf disease of tea in Sri Lanka, particularly devastating in high-elevation regions. The disease appears as circular blister-like swellings on young leaves, initially pale green then developing white powdery spore masses on the undersurface. Severe infections cause leaf distortion, defoliation, and significant yield loss. Favorable conditions include cool temperatures (15-20°C), high humidity, and continuous wet weather - conditions common in up country regions during monsoon periods. Infected leaves produce poor quality tea with off-flavors. Management includes resistant cultivars (TRI 2025, TRI 3019, TRI 4006, TRI 5001-5004), copper fungicide applications, and cultural practices promoting air circulation. Climate-smart cultivar selection is increasingly important as weather patterns shift.

documents.title: Root-Lesion Nematode in Tea
documents.content: Root-lesion nematode (Pratylenchus loosi) is a significant pest affecting tea productivity throughout Sri Lanka. These microscopic worms attack tea roots, causing lesions that impair nutrient and water uptake. Above-ground symptoms include stunted growth, yellowing leaves, poor recovery after pruning, and progressive decline. Nematode damage is often mistaken for nutrient deficiency or drought stress. Heavily infested fields may lose 20-40% of potential yield. The pest is particularly problematic in replanting situations where new plants are established in infested soil. Management options include tolerant cultivars (TRI 2025, TRI 4052, TRI 4053, TRI 5003), soil fumigation before replanting, and organic matter applications that encourage nematode-suppressing soil organisms. Nematode-free planting material is essential for new establishments.

documents.title: Shot Hole Borer Beetle
documents.content: Shot hole borer (Euwallacea fornicatus) is an ambrosia beetle that attacks tea stems, causing significant damage in Sri Lankan plantations. The beetle bores small circular holes into woody stems to cultivate fungal gardens that feed their larvae. This damage weakens branches, disrupts nutrient flow, and can cause dieback of affected sections. Heavy infestations kill entire bushes. Stressed plants are more susceptible - drought, poor nutrition, and heavy plucking increase vulnerability. Signs include small entry holes, sawdust accumulation, wilting of affected branches, and fungal staining of wood. Management includes removing and destroying affected branches, maintaining plant vigor, and using resistant cultivars. TRI 5001 shows notable resistance to shot hole borer, while TRI 5002-5004 are susceptible. Chemical control is difficult as beetles live inside stems.

documents.title: Red Spider Mite Damage
documents.content: Red spider mite (Oligonychus coffeae) causes significant foliar damage in tea, particularly during dry periods. These tiny arachnids feed on leaf undersurfaces, puncturing cells and extracting contents. Damage appears as bronze or reddish discoloration of upper leaf surfaces, with fine webbing visible underneath. Severe infestations cause defoliation and reduced photosynthesis, impacting both yield and quality. Hot, dry conditions favor mite population explosions - outbreaks often follow drought periods. Natural enemies including predatory mites help control populations in balanced ecosystems. Chemical control is sometimes necessary but risks disrupting beneficial organisms. Cultural practices including shade management, irrigation during drought, and avoiding excessive nitrogen fertilization help prevent outbreaks. Mite-damaged leaves should be excluded from harvest as they produce poor quality tea.

documents.title: Sri Lanka Tea Industry Statistics
documents.content: Sri Lanka is the fourth largest tea producer globally and second largest exporter of orthodox tea. The industry encompasses approximately 188,000 hectares of tea cultivation, producing around 298,000 tonnes annually. Tea accounts for approximately 15% of agricultural GDP and provides direct employment to over 1 million people, with indirect employment reaching 2 million. Sri Lanka holds approximately 19% of world tea export market share. The industry includes both large estates (plantations over 10 hectares) and smallholders (under 10 hectares). Smallholders now contribute over 75% of national production and often achieve higher per-hectare productivity than estates. The sector faces challenges including labor shortages, aging tea bushes, climate change impacts, and market price volatility. Diversification into value-added products and specialty teas is an ongoing strategic priority.

documents.title: Ceylon Tea Value and Pricing
documents.content: Ceylon tea consistently commands premium prices in global markets due to quality reputation and geographic indication protection. The Lion Logo trademark guarantees authentic Sri Lankan origin and quality standards. High-grown teas from Nuwara Eliya and Uva achieve the highest prices, particularly during quality seasons. Silver Tips sells for up to $1,500-2,000 per kilogram at auction. Premium BOPF from high-grown regions may reach $4-8 per kilogram compared to $2-3 for low-grown grades. Price is determined at the weekly Colombo Tea Auction, one of the world's largest tea auctions, where approximately 6 million kilograms trade weekly. Direct sales and private contracts increasingly bypass auction for specialty teas. Single-origin, estate-specific teas command premiums as consumers seek traceability and terroir character similar to wine appreciation.

documents.title: Tea Export Markets for Sri Lanka
documents.content: Sri Lankan tea exports reach over 150 countries, with major markets including Russia, Iran, Iraq, Turkey, UAE, and Syria. The Middle East and CIS countries together absorb over 50% of Ceylon tea exports. Japan and China represent growing markets for premium orthodox teas. Western markets including the UK, Germany, and USA value Ceylon tea for blending and increasingly for specialty single-origin products. Market preferences vary significantly - Middle Eastern consumers prefer strong teas, Japanese prefer lighter character, while Europeans value balanced profiles. Sri Lanka's orthodox production focus differentiates it from volume-oriented CTC producers in Kenya and India. Export promotion emphasizes quality, geographic indication, and health benefits. Challenges include competition from lower-priced origins and changing consumer preferences toward green tea and alternatives.

documents.title: Sustainable Tea Production Practices
documents.content: Sustainable tea production has become increasingly important for market access and long-term viability. Key certification schemes include Rainforest Alliance, Fairtrade, UTZ, and organic certifications. These programs address environmental impacts including agrochemical use, water management, biodiversity conservation, and carbon footprint. Social sustainability encompasses fair wages, worker welfare, community development, and gender equity. Economic sustainability requires profitable pricing that supports quality investment. Sri Lankan estates increasingly adopt integrated pest management reducing chemical inputs. Shade trees provide habitat corridors and improve growing conditions. Soil conservation measures address erosion on steep terrain. Renewable energy adoption is increasing in tea factories. Consumer demand for sustainably produced tea creates market incentives supporting these practices.

documents.title: Climate Change Impact on Tea
documents.content: Climate change poses significant threats to tea cultivation in Sri Lanka through altered rainfall patterns, temperature increases, and more frequent extreme weather events. Traditional quality seasons may shift as monsoon timing changes. Higher temperatures increase pest and disease pressure while potentially reducing quality in some regions. Drought events impact yield and make plants vulnerable to secondary stresses. Intense rainfall causes soil erosion and waterlogging. High-elevation regions may initially benefit from warming but face long-term uncertainty. Adaptation strategies include drought-tolerant cultivars, shade tree establishment, soil conservation, improved irrigation, and pest monitoring systems. Research focuses on understanding climate impacts and developing resilient production systems. The industry must balance short-term productivity with long-term climate adaptation.

documents.title: Tea Quality Assessment Methods
documents.content: Professional tea quality assessment involves systematic evaluation of dry leaf appearance, infused leaf, and liquor characteristics. Dry leaf is assessed for color uniformity, tip content, particle size consistency, and absence of fiber or foreign matter. The standard tasting protocol uses 2.86 grams of tea infused in 140ml boiling water for exactly 5 minutes. Liquor evaluation covers color, brightness, strength, briskness, body, and quality. Infused leaf assessment reveals processing quality and plucking standard. Professional tasters develop vocabularies including hundreds of descriptive terms. Quality factors are graded numerically for auction cataloguing. Cup quality, combined with leaf appearance, determines price. Geographic origin, season, and elevation influence expected character. The AI grading system aims to automate initial quality sorting, reserving human expertise for final quality determination.

documents.title: Factors Affecting Tea Quality
documents.content: Tea quality results from complex interactions among genetic, environmental, and processing factors. Cultivar determines baseline potential for quality attributes. Elevation profoundly affects quality - higher elevations produce more complex, delicate teas due to slower growth and cooler temperatures. Season influences quality with dry periods generally producing better teas than wet seasons. Plucking standard is critical - fine plucking yields superior tea while coarse plucking produces poor quality regardless of other factors. Soil nutrition affects plant health and leaf composition. Processing skill transforms raw material into finished tea - withering, rolling, oxidation, and drying must each be optimized. Storage conditions preserve or degrade quality over time. From bush to cup, every stage offers opportunities to enhance or diminish quality. Consistent quality requires control across this entire chain.

documents.title: AI Tea Leaf Quality Grading System
documents.content: The AI-driven tea leaf quality grading system developed for Project 25-26J-133 uses computer vision and machine learning to classify tea shoots into five quality categories. Fresh_Bud_1 (score: 10) represents premium quality with intact bud and 1-2 tender leaves. Fresh_Bud_2 (score: 8) indicates good quality with 2-3 leaves and bud. Coarse_Pluck (score: 0) identifies reject material with 3+ mature leaves. Old_Leaf (score: 0) detects overmature, yellowing leaves. Damaged_Leaf (score: 0) recognizes physical damage, pest holes, or disease symptoms. The classification follows TRI plucking standards and uses a priority-based decision hierarchy: damage is checked first, then age indicators, maturity, and finally freshness. This system aims to provide objective, consistent grading at scale while reducing reliance on human assessment variability.

documents.title: Visual Characteristics for AI Classification
documents.content: The AI grading system uses specific visual characteristics to classify tea shoots. Fresh_Bud_1 features visible unopened or slightly opened bud, light green color indicating freshness, soft pliable texture, and no damage or discoloration. Fresh_Bud_2 shows bud present but more open, 2-3 leaves attached, medium green color, and generally soft texture with minor imperfections acceptable. Coarse_Pluck displays no visible bud or very old bud, large mature leaves, dark green color, and thick woody stems. Old_Leaf exhibits yellowing or very dark coloration, stiff hardened texture, no bud present, and leathery appearance. Damaged_Leaf shows visible pest holes, brown or black disease spots, mechanical damage or tears, bruising or discoloration, and possibly fungal growth. These visual markers align with TRI quality assessment criteria and enable automated grading consistent with human expert evaluation.

documents.title: Quality Scoring and Batch Assessment
documents.content: The AI quality scoring system assigns numerical values enabling quantitative quality assessment. Premium leaves (Fresh_Bud_1) score 10 points, good quality (Fresh_Bud_2) scores 8 points, while reject categories (Coarse_Pluck, Old_Leaf, Damaged_Leaf) score 0 points. Batch quality is calculated as the weighted average: sum of individual scores divided by total leaves, multiplied by 10 for a 0-100 scale. For example, a batch of 10 leaves with 3 Fresh_Bud_1, 4 Fresh_Bud_2, and 3 Coarse_Pluck yields: (3×10 + 4×8 + 3×0)/10 × 10 = 62 points. Quality grades based on score ranges: A (80-100) Premium, B (60-80) Good, C (40-60) Standard, D (20-40) Below Standard, F (0-20) Reject. This quantitative approach enables consistent quality tracking and process optimization.

documents.title: Origins of Ceylon Tea Industry
documents.content: The Ceylon tea industry emerged from the ashes of coffee cultivation following the devastating coffee rust epidemic (Hemileia vastatrix) in the 1860s-1880s that destroyed the island's coffee plantations. Scottish planter James Taylor established the first commercial tea plantation at Loolecondera Estate in Kandy district in 1867, planting seeds from Assam, India. Taylor's experimental plot of 19 acres expanded rapidly as coffee estates converted to tea. By 1872, Taylor had built his first tea factory using Chinese processing methods adapted to local conditions. The first shipment of Ceylon tea reached London in 1873. Thomas Lipton's investment in the 1890s helped popularize Ceylon tea globally. By 1900, tea had completely replaced coffee as Ceylon's primary agricultural export. The industry's rapid development was facilitated by existing plantation infrastructure, labor force, and transportation networks established during the coffee era.

documents.title: Evolution of Ceylon Tea Processing
documents.content: Tea processing in Ceylon evolved from crude manual methods to sophisticated mechanized operations. James Taylor's early techniques adapted Chinese methods with local innovations. The introduction of the Sirocco dryer in 1877 revolutionized drying operations. Rolling machines replaced hand-rolling in the 1880s, enabling larger scale production. British engineer W. Jackson invented the roller specifically for Ceylon conditions. Withering troughs with fan systems replaced natural withering, providing consistent results regardless of weather. The orthodox processing method was standardized during this period, becoming Ceylon's signature approach. While CTC processing was adopted elsewhere in the 20th century, Sri Lanka maintained orthodox focus, preserving traditional quality character. Modern factories combine historical knowledge with contemporary technology including automated fermentation monitoring and computer-controlled drying. This evolution balanced efficiency gains with quality preservation.

documents.title: Colombo Tea Auction
documents.content: The Colombo Tea Auction is one of the world's largest and most important tea trading centers, handling approximately 6 million kilograms weekly. Established in 1883 during the colonial era, the auction operates every Tuesday at the Ceylon Chamber of Commerce. Sellers present samples catalogued by estate, grade, and quality descriptors. Licensed brokers conduct tasting sessions before auction day. Bidding is rapid - experienced buyers make split-second decisions based on sample quality and market intelligence. Prices established at Colombo influence global tea markets. The auction system provides price discovery, market access for producers of all sizes, and quality-based competition. Digital innovations are modernizing auction processes while maintaining the fundamental price discovery function. Approximately 60% of Sri Lankan tea trades through auction, with remainder sold through private contracts and direct export arrangements.

documents.title: Ceylon Tea Trademarks and Certification
documents.content: The Ceylon Tea Trademark featuring the Lion Logo is one of the world's oldest tea certification marks, owned and administered by the Sri Lanka Tea Board. This trademark guarantees that tea originates from Sri Lanka, was processed in Sri Lanka, and meets minimum quality standards. The Lion Logo symbol features a lion holding a sword within a distinctive shape. Licensed packers must meet strict criteria including quality control systems, proper storage facilities, and compliance with food safety standards. The trademark helps combat counterfeit products and protects Ceylon tea's premium reputation. Additional geographic indicators specify regional origin - Nuwara Eliya, Uva, Dimbula, Kandy, Ruhuna - for single-origin marketing. Fair Trade, Rainforest Alliance, and organic certifications provide additional assurance for consumers seeking sustainably produced tea. These trademarks and certifications create trust and justify premium pricing.

Introduction Diseases, insect, mite and nematode pests, and weeds occur in tea, in different stages of the crop, and at different times of the year. Rational use of fungicides, insecticides, acaricides, nematicides and weedicides is a part of integrated management of diseases, insects, mites, nematodes and weeds respectively. It has become necessary to introduce mechanization to tea plantations since the tea sector is presently facing acute worker shortage. Mechanization in agriculture is the use of machine to accomplish a task or operation involved in agricultural production. Key objectives of mechanization are to increase worker productivity, reduc e cost of production, improv e product quality, eas e manual operations, complete tasks timely and change worker attitudes. Tea planting system facilitating mechanization of field operations Mechanization of field operations requires adequate space for worker and machine mobility, dense canopy architecture and absence of obstacles such as shade trees in the path of machine operation. The tea is cultivated in the tea gardens of the delimitated geographical area of the island of Sri Lanka. 1. Tea species are exclusively Camelia sinensis. 2. Tea bushes are either multiplied by vegetative propagation (VPs) or seedlings. 3. Tea gardens must be well maintained through good agricultural practices. 4. All new planting and replanting of seedlings or VPs should ensure good shade management. Shade trees are important element of tea gardens as they simulate forest conditions, which are the natural habitat of tea. Shade trees provide additional environmental co-benefits important for the sustainability of tea gardens, especially in the context of climate change. 5. Weed management must follow the Integrated Weed Management (IWM) system. Herbicides/weedicides/pesticides use must respect a minimum interval of one week before

The Integrated Weed Management (IWM) approach includes preventive, manual, biological, cultural, mechanical and chemical methods (in rotation) as defined by the most current TRI circular on Weed Management. Tea gardens must limit chemical weeding to levels of inputs and application frequency as defined by the up-to-date version of the TRI advisory circular on Chemical control of weeds in tea lands. 4.2/ Plucking 0. The tea bushes are plucked at required intervals of 6 to 10 days to ensure a regular renewal of juvenile leaves and a bud. 1. Plucking can be done by hand or by a mechanical device. A sub-labelling of “Hand plucked” can be used for tea that is 100% hand plucked. 2. Plucking standard is systematically determined at factory gate according to the three categories of plucking standards defined in the “quality of the raw material” (part 3.2) 4.3/ Transport of green leaf 0. The green leaves must be transported in a way to preserve the quality of the leaves from farm gate (or collection point) to factory. 1. Green leaves must be delivered to the factory before 8:30PM on the same day they have been plucked. 2. Green leaf transport must be done with one or more approved containers recommended by the Tea Commissioner if located from and more than 5 km from the factory: 1. Plastic crates with a maximum load of 20 kg. 17 2. Coir sacks (80cm x 65cm - minimum size) with a maximum load of 18 kg. 3. Nylon sacks (90cm x 70cm) with a maximum load of 20 kg. 4. Transport vehicles must be adapted and equipped for the transport of fresh green tea leaves. Collection lorries must be ventilated and equipped with racks and/or shelves for sacks handling. There should also be protection against the rain.

There are different types of tea commonly manufactured in the region: 0. Black tea: pure Orthodox, Orthodox-Rotorvane, CTC 1. Green tea 2. White tea, silver tips, golden tips 4.4.1/ Black tea Black tea is produced from the green leaves, by the following processes - notably withering, leaf maceration, aeration and drying. There are 3 sub-categories of black tea, each based on a type of manufacturing: 1. Orthodox black tea, which produces leafy and broken tea grades 2. Orthodox-Rotorvane black tea, which produces broken tea grades 3. CTC (Cut, tear, curl), which produces predominantly small and even tea grades Withering: upon arrival at the factory, the leaves are checked for quality (cf. 3.2) and the required quantity is weighed and loaded on withering troughs. Air is passed through the bed of leaves to reduce its moisture content to 55 – 60% (w/w, wet basis) in Pure Orthodox & Orthodox-Rotorvane type of manufacturing and 18 to 68-70% (w/w, wet basis) in CTC manufacturing. A minimum of 6 hours of withering is required for necessary chemical changes in leaves. Figure: leaf quality check Figure: withering lines: Rolling: the withered leaves are then transferred/directed from the withering section to the rolling section. They are then twisted, which, by subjecting the withered leaves to a rolling movement under pressure, twist the leaves, rupture the cells and release cell sap, promoting oxidation and accelerating pigmentation. 19 For the production of Orthodox-Rotorvane black tea, a slight variation happens at the rolling step where Rotorvanes are used to macerate the leaves after the step of rolling in orthodox roller. A blight, also called the coffee rust, showed first signs in 1869 and subsequently wiped out the coffee production in the span of a decade1. Witnessing the devastating effects of the coffee rust, coffee planters soon started looking for an alternative commercial crop. After years of experimental cultivation and processing of tea at the border of his coffee estate of Loolecandera near Kandy and attempts to match the know-how of Assam tea planters, the Scottish planter James Taylor established the first commercial tea plantation in 1867. He was the first planter in Ceylon to succeed with tea but he was not the first to try. Though records are scant, there is evidence that the cultivation of tea plants imported from China was attempted as early as 18242. Tea presented

documents.title: Specification – Ceylon tea (Part 14)
documents.content: numerous advantages. Tea bushes are well-suited to tropical climate and hilly topography of the island and public and private existing infrastructure, initially geared to the requirements of the coffee enterprise, could be adapted rapidly to serve the needs of tea. By the end of the century, the emerging tea industry soon surpassed all successes of its coffee predecessor in terms of export volumes, revenues and area under cultivation3. 6.2/ Historical reputation of ‘Ceylon tea’ 6.2.1/ ‘Ceylon tea’ name Under British rule, from 1815 to 1948, Sri Lanka was known as Ceylon, a name it kept for nearly a quarter-century after independence. The English name Ceylon is derived from Sihala, which is a poor rendering of the Sinhalese name of the island. The Arabic name(s) – Serendip, Serendiv, Singaldip - is derived from Sinhaladvipa. Similarly, the Greek name – Sheelan, Sielen Diva and ‘Salike’ also derived from the name Sinhala - the land of the Sinhalas. From the name Sielen, many European forms were derived: the Portuguese Ceilão, Spanish Ceilán, Dutch Zeilan, Ceilan, Seylon; French Selon, Ceylan and the Latin Zeylan. Ceylon gained independence on the 4 February 1948. In 1972, a new constitution was enacted, and Ceylon became the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka. However, the name ‘Ceylon’ remained for the most famous national ‘brands’, such as tea or cinnamon. Indeed, the name ‘Ceylon tea’ has been used in trade since the 1880s4. At present, the Sri Lanka tea industry involves more than 397,233 smallholdings (2005) and 328 tea estates (293 in RPCs & 35 in States) (MAPI, 2018); 1,596 registered tea leaf dealers; 782 active registered factories; 8 registered tea brokers; 386 registered tea exporters and 189 registered packers (Sri Lanka Tea Board (SLTB, 2022)). 1 History of Ceylon Tea | Sri Lanka Tea Board. https://www.srilankateaboard.lk/ceylon-tea/history-of-ceylon-tea/. documents.content: specificities of the delimitated geographical area gives ‘Ceylon tea’ both physical and organoleptic recognizable characteristics. Located on a tropical island (between 5° 55' to 9° 51' North latitude and between 79° 42' to 81° 53' East longitude) ‘Ceylon tea’ cultivation extends over an altitude gradient ranging from sea level up to high altitudes (above 1200 meters). In the tea sector, it is therefore common to refer first to ‘Ceylon tea’ growing area by their altitude, namely: the “low country” (ranging from sea level to 600m), “mid country” (600m to 1200m) and “up country” (above 1200m). The agro-climatic specificities of ‘Ceylon tea’ are defined by an important diversity in climate in the tea growing areas. This is a signification feature in the wet and intermediate zones of Sri Lanka. The rainfall pattern is distinctly seasonal with two pics. More specifically, rainfalls are paced by the South-West monsoon from May to September, and the North-East monsoon from December to February, followed by inter-monsoonal rains covering the whole island (March-April and October-November). The central mountains act as a divider between those two annual climatic events, which results in different periods of rainfall on either side of the mountains. The amount of rainfall and its distributions are the most important factors that affect the productivity of tea. The number of rainless days in the wet zone is very small compared to the total number of rainy days in a year. In addition, the agro-climatic conditions of the delimited geographical area offer good exposition to solar radiation. The mean annual sunshine duration in the wet zone ranges from 4.9 to 6.4 hours per day depending on the location. The above-mentioned criteria, combined with soil conditions, terrain and land use pattern, defines 46 Agro-Ecological Regions (AERs) for the whole of Sri Lanka (see Map of agro-ecological

Plucking - Most of ‘Ceylon tea’ is harvested or plucked manually. The particular know-how of tea pluckers allows them to select the best leaves to produce quality ‘Ceylon tea’. The tea pluckers master different types of plucking techniques to identify the good leaves to be plucked, foster the productivity of the tea bush and support the maintenance of the tea bushes22. Tea manufacture - The quality of ‘Ceylon tea’ is the result of a dense network of tea factories, which gradually developed a tea manufacturing process to optimize natural, agronomic, logistic and economic conditions. When tea bushes replaced dying coffee plants, tea factories were built on-site to allow processing of raw leaves, in order to maintain their freshness and quality. Colombo Auction – The auction system can be considered as part of the cultural heritage that showcases the ‘Ceylon tea’ quality and contributes to its truthful recognition. Tea auctions were first introduced in Colombo in 1883, on the premises of Somerville & Co., a Colombo merchant house, on the basis of those conducted at Mincing Lane in London. By the turn of the century, most of the estates were owned by joint-stock companies, either listed in sterling or in rupee. Shareholders of those companies were British, often far from the plantations. The management in the estates was delegated to ‘management companies’ or ‘agency houses’, which handled the cultivation, processing and sale of tea. In Colombo, the agency houses employed teams of expert tea-tasters to sample and report on the quality of each estate’s produce before it was put up for auction in Colombo or London. The brokers and buyers, too, had their tasters, and it was tasters from both sides who attended the auctions. Once established, the structure of the ‘tea trade’ was little altered. Overseen by trade associations such as the Ceylon Chamber of Commerce (est. 1839) and the Colombo Tea Traders’ Association (est. 1894), it continued to function with little change in operational procedure, management style or ownership structure throughout the colonial period and was British-dominated23. The Colombo tea auction in Sri Lanka now operates as an online platform; the first historical online auction was successfully conducted on 4 April 2020. Tea Blending and Flavouring – The specificity of ‘Ceylon tea’ is evident in the wide range of tastes and flavours derived from the diversity of the agro-ecological regions in which it is found. As a result, the ‘Ceylon tea’ sector has developed recognized know-how in terms of tea identification and blending, to obtain the desired appearance, qualities and aromatic notes in the final beverage. Tea tasters have an important role in factories and brokers and exporters’ houses. They are specifically trained for quality assessment. Experienced tea tasters can identify defects, their origin and consequently advise the manufacturer regarding over or under firing, over or under fermentation/oxidation, over or under withering, etc. They are also trained to recognise the special regional characters of ‘Ceylon tea’ as well as the wide range of grades. Therefore, like tea factory quality officers, tea tasters are defenders of an origin and taste that make the quality of ‘Ceylon tea’ special. Blends of teas from Sri Lanka and flavouring in Sri Lanka are important features of ‘Ceylon tea’ exporters’ specific know-how. As described earlier, blending of teas from Sri Lanka and flavouring is traditionally done in Sri Lanka to produce ‘Ceylon tea’. It is a currently established practice to flavour the tea. Flavour like bergamot is ancient, whereas botanicals is more recent. Exporters tend to respond to customers’ requests for a specific taste, smell and appearance (colour and shape) of the tea. Exporters build standards, which act as references to respond to those requirements. DSLS 1523 Part 9: ………. 3 Draft Sri Lanka Standard REQUIREMENTS FOR GOOD AGRICULTURAL PRACTICES (GAP) PART 9: TEA FOREWORD This Standard was approved by the Sectoral Committee on Agriculture and was authorized for adoption and publication as a Sri Lanka Standard by the Council of the Sri Lanka Standards Institution on ……………………….. This standard is one of a series of standards on Good Agricultural Practices (GAP) to be developed. Tea (Camellia sinensis) cultivated, managed, maintained, harvested and processed as a health benefiting and stimulating beverage and a prime trade commodity constitutes an important part of Sri Lankan life and economics being a major export item. In the new trade regime, there are significant divergences in the consumer behavior worldwide with regard to the product they consume. Consumers are increasingly concerned with the conditions in which the products they consume are produced. Therefore, many importing countries and local buyers are now necessitating producers and practitioners to implement Good Agricul tural Practices (GAPs) as a pre-requisite for procurement to ensure quality and safety of the produce. To build trust and recognition of the produce to be accepted both in the domestic and international markets by considering the environment, health and fo od safety of consumers, quality of produce and welfare of the workers, it is appropriate to establish the GAP Standard for tea. The GAP stands on four pillars of economic feasibility, environmental sustainability, social acceptability, and food safety and quality. Therefore, GAP will serve as a guideline for the management of tea value chain aiming at ensuring safety in the crop produce for both domestic
